Programs are a set of sequential instructions/steps written with the assumption that one is done before the next.

Using multiple processors is splitting up those instruction sets to different processors/cores.

Laziness would be part of the equation. You have to program the computer to use those extra cores, and that isn't always a priority. It's usually simpler to just run one thread, which means that's the cheapest and least error prone way to write code. Unless you have a reason, you don't want to pay your programmers to spend extra time getting the code to run extra cores, and even more time debugging it. And extra cores won't always provide significant performance improvement. On mobile devices running extra cores will drain the battery more quickly too.

I think this is the biggest reason.

1. Not all problems can be 'parallelised' - sorting large data sets can, but running difference equations can not.
  2. Extra effort needed to avoid problems due to concurrent access, which can itself introduce bugs which cause blocking (proper planning is everything!).
  3. Many programs do use multiple threads, though only one thread is working actively. For example, if a program is doing a CPU-intensive operation while still showing a responsive interface with progress %, having 2 physical cores is buying you a nice user experience.

Using multiple processors is like using multiple people to get a single job done. It's only faster if it is a job that can be done by multiple people, and a lot of times the work of organizing all the different people is more effort than the work of doing the entire job yourself.

To be clear, the issue is that processor cores are only faster when they are NOT sharing information with each other. Any time they need to talk to each other they pretty much stop every process and wait for each other to catch up, and then sync everything. The only way around this is to architect a process for them to communicate asynchronously.

Building a car is a great job for multi-threading. You think of each person as a thread, one of them takes a part off the queue, performs an action on it, and puts the modified part onto the next queue for another person to work on. That's an assembly line and it makes the entire process faster.
